content:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Heineken’s memo about effects of weight-loss drugs on drinking, RNDC’s Chapter 11 liquidation, and a ton of product releases.

News to know:

  • Heineken alarms U.K. pubs of GLP-1 effects on booze purchases: Heineken warned of weight-loss drugs’ negative effects on alcohol purchases and suggested strategies for working around them in a document sent to U.K. bars and pubs. The document, unsealed and reviewed by Reuters, marks one of the few times a major alcohol company has addressed potential setbacks to business caused by GLP-1s — earlier this year, executives at Diageo and Carlsberg both played down the suspicion that the drugs significantly curb alcohol consumption. Heineken, the second largest brewer in the world, urged pub and bar operators to serve half-pints, low- and non-alcoholic drinks, and smaller food plates.
  • Judge OKs RNDC’s Chapter 11 plan after settlement with unsecured creditors: A Texas judge approved Republic National Distributing Company’s (RNDC) Chapter 11 liquidation plan on Tuesday after the company reached a settlement with its unsecured creditors last week. RNDC, once the second-largest alcohol distributor in the U.S. before shedding nearly all of its business this past year, filed for bankruptcy in July.
  • Court denies Fawn Weaver’s motion to block Uncle Nearest sale: A U.S. court rejected Weaver’s motion to stop the sale of her embattled whiskey brand. Weaver filed the request for injunction earlier this month after Uncle Nearest’s court-appointed receiver Phillip G. Young, Jr., noted three potential buyers were actively eyeing the brand in a separate court filing.
  • Class suit brewing against Celsius’ “burns body fat” claims: A Washington State resident sued Celsius over “healthwashing” for making unsubstantiated claims that the energy drink “burns body fat.” The plaintiff Annabelle Nielsen is hoping to loop in other consumers to launch a class action lawsuit.

Product releases to watch:

  • Popular Prosecco brand adds first sparkling non-alcoholic wine to portfolio: La Marca, the top-selling Prosecco brand in the U.S., released its first-ever zero-proof sparkling wine. Made with carbonated de-alcoholized wine, the NA version of the beloved crisp, fruity bubbly is available nationwide for a suggested retail price of $18.99 per bottle.
  • 1792 releases a wheated, full-proof bourbon: The Bardstown, Ky.-based brand rolled out a wheated bourbon bottled at 125 proof. 1792 Wheated Full Proof Bourbon will be available next month in California, Florida, Illinois, Texas, and New York, for a suggested retail price of $39.99 per 375-milliliter bottle.
  • Four Roses debuted third Experimental Series bourbon: Four Roses’ latest addition to its Experimental Series is a bourbon finished in Japanese chestnut wood. Experimental Series No. 003: Chestnut is bottled at 104 proof and will be available at the Lawrenceburg and Cox’s Creek, Ky., visitor centers beginning Nov. 20 for a suggested retail price of $55 per 375-milliliter bottle.
  • The Whistler’s ‘Triple Oak’ blends three different whiskeys aged in three different casks: The Irish Whiskey brand’s newest release combines single pot still, single malt, and single grain whiskeys aged in ex-bourbon, Oloroso sherry, and PX sherry casks, respectively. The Whistler Triple Oak is now available nationwide for a suggested retail price of $29.99.
  • Blade and Bow bottles 30-year-old bourbon at cask strength: Blade and Bow unveiled a cask-strength expression of its esteemed 30-year bourbon. The limited release was distilled in 1993 and bottled three decades later at 164.2 proof. Just 30 bottles of the Blade and Bow 30-Year-Old Cask Strength will be available at the Stitzel-Weller Distillery beginning Oct. 30 for $2,500, followed by limited, drop-style releases to select markets.

title: After Going Mainstream, Has Pumpkin Beer Become a Regional Specialty Again?
summary:

content:
Earlier this month, Jack’s Abby Brewing in Framingham, Mass., cranked up the oom-pah tunes for Oktoberfest revelry featuring stein-hoisting contests, plump pretzels, and lots and lots of lager.

“We set our all-time sales record for the beer hall,” says Sam Hendler, CEO of parent company Hendler Family Brewing.

Unsurprisingly, golden Munich Fest and Copper Legend Oktoberfest lagers took the top draft sales slots. Third place welcomed an underdog: Pumpkin Crop, a spiced autumnal lager. “That’s different from 10 years ago when it was all German lagers at Oktoberfest,” Hendler says. Now people want to party with pumpkin beer. When it comes to drinkers losing their gourd, “Massachusetts is a pretty good bellwether for New England.”

Pumpkin beer’s popularity in New England dates to Colonial America when resourceful brewers embraced pumpkins as a cheap and plentiful fermentable. During craft beer’s late-20th century rise, the region’s breweries rebooted pumpkin ale as a spiced fall seasonal that tasted like boozy pumpkin pie.

“You can almost call it the original pastry beer,” says Phil Markowski, the brewmaster at Two Roads Brewing in Stratford, Conn.

Pumpkin beer hit a rough patch in the mid-2010s when market saturation and summertime releases sparked a backlash. Many pumpkin beers disappeared, but the style held strong in New England, fall’s wonderland of pumpkin patches, apple orchards, and leaf-peeping.

“These iconic seasonal moments create appetite and excitement for beers that echo the flavors and feelings of fall,” says Jon London, the head of beer at Boston Beer Company, which makes cinnamon-spiced Sam Adams Jack-O pumpkin ale.

Instead of dying on the vine, pumpkin beer today thrives as a regional specialty with deep-rooted preferences for time-tested brands. Born in 1996, Shipyard Brewing’s Pumpkinhead Ale still shines from its Portland, Maine headquarters down the East Coast. Across the country, Seattle’s Elysian Brewing first brewed the spiced Night Owl Pumpkin Ale in 1997, and the brand returns every fall.

“We love traditions and are creatures of habit, aren’t we?” says Jeff Richards, the senior marketing director at Elysian. “Pumpkin beer is one part of how we share in the spirit of the season.”

Why New England Is Awash in Pumpkin Beers

No region loves pumpkin beers more than New England. Over the past five years, Google Trends data show a concentration of interest in New England, with a pronounced spike this year. “Fall seasonal beers are more popular in New England than other areas of the country,” a Total Wine rep reported via email.

Pumpkin beer is “built into the culture,” says Rob Day, the vice president of marketing for Barrel One Collective, which encompasses 15 mainly New England brands including Harpoon, Smuttynose, Wachusett, and Long Trail. “People look forward to these moments.”

Barrel One sells seven different pumpkin beers and ciders, many with regional affinity. New Hampshire enjoys Smuttynose Pumpkin Ale, New Yorkers order Five Boroughs Pumpkin Ale, and Massachusetts drinkers crush Wachusett Pumpkin Ale.

“In each state, there’s a different pumpkin product in our portfolio that’s outperforming,” Day says. Sales of UFO Pumpkin are up 18 percent in Rhode Island, while Harpoon Pumpkin Cider is up 9.3 percent in Connecticut and Clown Shoes Pumpkin Sombrero is up 28 percent in New Hampshire.

“Fall seasonal beers are more popular in New England than other areas of the country.”

Pumpkin beer drinkers aren’t monolithic. For Hendler Family’s Massachusetts brands, flavor and ABV preferences vary across customer bases. Night Shift’s potent and strongly flavored Pumpkin Piescraper appeals to a younger, more urban crowd, Hendler shares, while Wormtown’s mellower, lower-alcohol Fresh Patch hits the blue-collar, more suburban customer base.

“The pumpkin beer phenomenon works across all demographics in Massachusetts,” Hendler says.

In Massachusetts, this fall’s most popular pumpkin beer is Shipyard Pumpkinhead, according to Circana data. “That’s our biggest market,” says Bruce Forsley, Shipyard’s president. Now 30 years old, Pumpkinhead accounts for almost half of Shipyard’s annual production and remains steady. “Craft beer has been struggling the last few years, but this segment remains healthy and robust with no immediate signs of decline,” Forsley says.

Shipyard is singularly focused on expanding and supporting the Pumpkinhead franchise. Smashed Pumpkin, the 9 percent ABV imperial pumpkin ale, continues to grow, and there’s also a version aged in bourbon barrels. This year, Shipyard also introduced an NA Pumpkinhead that sold out in three weeks. “We vastly underestimated the NA beer market,” says Forsley, who plans to boost production next year.

Pumpkin’s Fandom Spreads Wide

Thriving pockets of fandom expand beyond the Northeast, too, in part fueled by legacy brands. Southern Tier Brewing in Lakewood, N.Y., has ardent fans of Pumking Imperial Ale (born 2007) in New York State and adjoining regions; and Dogfish Head in Milton, Del., has legions of mid-Atlantic fans for Punkin Ale, first brewed in 1994.

Despite national interest seemingly waning, pumpkin beer sales are actually increasing in several surprising pockets. Shipyard ships Pumpkinhead Ale to 42 states. Georgia is growing, and “Florida is a very good market because New England transplants are down there,” Forsley says.

The challenge with wide distribution is a shorter selling season in warm-weather states. Pumpkin ale can be a tough sell when it tops 100 degrees in Texas, so distributors want to sell the beer in two or three weeks. “There’s not a traditional fall season,” he says. “There’s just the thought that, This is the time of year when I should have this beer.”

Heatwaves, though, aren’t a dealbreaker. Total Wine & More reports that searches for pumpkin products ramp up around the end of July, with a 210 percent increase from July 2020 to July 2026. And that warm-weather arrival of pumpkin beers is a feature, not a bug, of the complex beer-distribution system and demands of the calendar. “Seasonal creep” is just standard operating procedure for large brewers that need lead time for brewing, packaging, and shipping.

“Our distributors, by and large, will bring Pumpkinhead in July to be prepared to release it as soon as they have sold their last case of the previous seasonal beer, which is summer,” Forsley says. Could be mid-August, or maybe late July. “It’s based on depletion.”

“Craft beer has been struggling the last few years, but this segment remains healthy and robust with no immediate signs of decline.”

Boston Beer typically releases its fall seasonals, including Jack-O, during the first week of August. “That’s when people start craving fall,” London says. In a competitive sales landscape, “we want to be first to market with the seasonals people are excited about.”

Selling pumpkin beer earlier gives breweries a headstart on the style’s unofficial October 31 end date. “Even though pumpkin carries into Thanksgiving in such a big way, Halloween kind of ends pumpkin beer and you’re on your way out,” Day says.

Pumpkin Is an Invitation to Party

Encouraging customers to party maximizes the compressed sales season. This October, Two Roads hosted its eighth annual Roadsmary’s Baby Pumpkin Fest to celebrate its pumpkin beer partly aged in rum barrels. Attendees competed in pumpkin-carving competitions, watched The Ring, and ate pumpkin pie.

“The Northeast is known for pumpkin celebrations,” Markowski says, adding that Roadsmary’s Baby remains the top-selling Two Roads seasonal. Though volumes are down around 50 percent from the pre-pandemic peak, Two Roads still sells more than 1,000 barrels annually. “It’s here to stay,” he says.

Early October also marked Elysian’s 22nd annual Great Pumpkin Beer Festival. Nearly 3,000 people attended the block party to drink pumpkin ale poured from a hollowed-out 1,700-pound pumpkin. “We sold more beer on that Saturday night than we’ve ever sold on any single GPBF day,” Richards says. One-off releases keep interest high. Elysian has produced more than 100 different pumpkin beers over the years, including a pumpkin cheesecake ale and a pumpkin sour ale.

“The ability to create novelty around the familiar each year is so cool,” he says.

Beer styles were once rooted in place and taste: crisply elegant kölsch in Cologne, Germany; acidic lambic in Brussels, Belgium; bitter West Coast IPAs in California. Now every beer can be made everywhere, recipes and processes replicated around the globe. Reverting pumpkin beers to regional specialties, only sold for a few short yet festive months, can rekindle what once made craft beer so special. Here’s a beer, only available for the here and now.

Check out Maine’s fall foliage, hit a pumpkin patch, then pop by a neighborhood bar for a Pumpkinhead pint rimmed with sugar and cinnamon. Says Forsley, “It’s truly an American experience.”

title: Why We Still Ask for a ‘Fifth’ at Liquor Shops, and the 1980 Law That Shrank U.S. Booze Bottles

content:
When it comes to measurements, most people — including Americans themselves — are eager to criticize the United States for its rejection of the metric system. Instead of embracing international units of measurement like liters, meters, and grams, the U.S. Customary System opts for units like gallons, inches, and pounds. But in one instance when the U.S. required a certain industry to make the pivot to metric, many citizens were not so pleased.

On Jan. 1, 1980, the federal government passed a law that mandated the American liquor industry adopt metric system norms, converting the volume measurements on all spirits bottles in the U.S. to liters. (A law required wine bottles to convert to metric units the previous year.) The U.S. made the switch in an effort to streamline trading booze across borders — a shift the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms had pushed for years.

But the law didn’t just change the numbers displayed on the side of each bottle — in changing the units, the booze industry also started producing an entirely new set of bottle sizes. And when the law went into effect at the start of 1980, observant shoppers noticed their go-to bottle of liquor had shrunk.

The bottles that notoriously took the hit were the “fifths,” which were popular among consumers for their convenient size and easy-to-remember name. Equal to one-fifth of a gallon, “fifths” came out to around 757 milliliters. But under the new law, those were replaced with 750 milliliter bottles to match the metric system’s standards. The law also instated five additional bottle volumes: 50 milliliters, 200 milliliters, 500 milliliters, 1 liter, and 1 ¾ liters.

A 7 milliliter decrease might seem like a drop in the bucket, and it is: A jigger equates to roughly 44 milliliters, meaning each fifth lost just a fraction of a shot. So, it might come as a surprise that the slight change in bottle size caused quite the uproar among consumers.

People were so outraged that the news usurped other, more impactful laws that came with the new decade — including a $0.20 raise to the federal minimum wage. The fifth was such a cultural touchpoint at the time that the alcohol industry’s new system dominated the conversation. On Dec. 31, 1979, the Washington Post published the headline “Era of the Fifth to End With New Year” and the subheadline “Introducing Smaller Fifths, Higher Taxes.”

While the switch to metric became mandatory in 1980, liquor companies began pivoting to the measurement system as early as 1976 as part of a multi-year effort to ease in the industry’s new sizings. Beyond “fifths,” others within the previous system had easy calling cards as well — such as “quart,” “half gallon,” and “gallon” — and over the course of those four transitional years, consumers and tradespeople alike were stuck in a firestorm over what to call the new sizes.

As the old sizes phased out, many pitched new monikers for customers to use when they entered a liquor store. For instance, the Distilled Council Spirits Council of the United States (DICSUS) proposed referring to 200-milliliter bottles as “miniatures,” whereas some distillers hoped for the term “flasks” to catch on. In 1976, the then-president of DISCUS told the New York Times, “There are myriad problems in this industry, and this is one of them. We wanted to have uniform nomenclature, but it doesn’t seem to be working out that way.” His suspicion rings true today: There still isn’t a set terminology for bottle sizes beyond “handle” for 1 ¾ liters and the “fifth,” which stuck despite the volume no longer measuring to one fifth of a gallon.

After all, the switch from 757 milliliters was just a minor shrink, and the 750 milliliters are nearly identical to what were once fifths. So, whenever you hear the calling card “fifth,” know that you aren’t getting one fifth of a gallon but rather one percent less.

title: We Asked 14 Bartenders: What Bottle Is a ‘Green Flag’ When You See It at a Bar? (2026)
summary:
When you visit a bar for the first time, there’s always a slight possibility you may leave disappointed. It’s a chance you’re willing to take if you’re a cocktail enthusiast, particularly if you’re dropping by a spot that’s generated its fair share of acclaim. But it’s also one that may leave you particularly frustrated these days when you have to invest $20-plus to try one cocktail. A “green flag” bottle on a bar’s back shelf can go a long way into mitigating any concerns you may have about the establishment’s quality.

The article We Asked 14 Bartenders: What Bottle Is a ‘Green Flag’ When You See It at a Bar? (2026) appeared first on VinePair.
content:
When you visit a bar for the first time, there’s always a slight possibility you may leave disappointed. It’s a chance you’re willing to take if you’re a cocktail enthusiast, particularly if you’re dropping by a spot that’s generated its fair share of acclaim. But it’s also one that may leave you particularly frustrated these days when you have to invest $20-plus to try one cocktail.

A “green flag” bottle on a bar’s back shelf can go a long way into mitigating any concerns you may have about the establishment’s quality. Spotting a specific brand or a slightly obscure label can provide a quick clue about a bar’s cocktail-making capabilities, commitment to quality, and staff nerdiness — elements you may find alluring if you fancy yourself a drinks buff. There are no set rules about what makes a bottle a positive sign. It could be a well-respected rum brand, a small-batch amaro, or even a slightly weird neon liqueur from three decades ago enjoying a market resurgence.

Nobody’s better at identifying these bottles than bartenders, since their job usually requires them to be familiar with a wide range of bottles spread across numerous categories. So what bottles are worthy of “green flag” status? We asked 14 bartenders to find out. Here’s what they had to say.

The green flag bottles behind the bar, according to bartenders:

  • Ron Del Barrilito 3 Star
  • Punt e Mes
  • Ron Abuelo Rum
  • Benriach Scotch
  • Chartreuse 1605
  • Hpnotiq
  • Cascahuín Tequila
  • See the Elephant Amaro
  • Galliano
  • Rochelt Brandy
  • Green Chartreuse
  • Yellow Chartreuse
  • Tapatio 110
  • Nikaido Shochu
  • Worthy Park 109

“Ron Del Barrilito 3 Star is my ultimate green flag to see when I walk into a bar. It’s always made in small batches, using original distillation methods dating back to 1880, and aged in Oloroso sherry casks for at least three to five years. It’s subtle, smoky, and woody, accentuated by notes of almond, vanilla, and plum. As we get into colder months, it’s my favorite spirit to drink neat, but it holds up equally well over a large rock. Seeing it on a back bar is an indication that the bar program is thoughtful and intentional, while still being accessible for all.” —Hannah Hulsey, head bartender, FKA: Formerly Known As, New York City

“There are a variety of craft cocktail shibboleths one sees in the great bars of the world, but none more important than Punt e Mes. Anyone opening a bar these days can figure out the obvious amari and monk-made liqueurs expected to line the shelves. Punt e Mes is a dive deeper. It is a product that needs experience to work with, and demands a fine touch. When a bottle of Punt e Mes comes out of the fridge and is skillfully measured into a Manhattan or Negroni riff you know you are sitting on a world-class barstool.“ —Toby Maloney, owner, The Elbow Room, Vancouver, Wash.

“Any spirit that’s got zero marketing budget but is high quality — stuff like Ron Abuelo rum or Benriach Scotch. To me, seeing those bottles tells me whoever curates the bar cares and hasn’t gone only for marketable overdone stuff.” —Patrick Chiquette, bartender, Le Grand Comité, Montreal

“Seeing a bottle of Chartreuse 1605 behind the bar is an instant green flag for me. It’s a special release bottle and not one you see often, and I love when a bar makes room for spirits that are a little more unique and have a story behind them. To me, it shows that whoever is putting the back bar together really appreciates what they’re working with. It’s a small detail that screams at serious enthusiasts, but it’s also the kind of thing that makes me appreciate a bar before I’ve even ordered a drink. It makes me pay closer attention to everything else they have to offer.” —Julian Flores Torres, beverage director, Mode Bar, Santa Ana, Calif.

“A bottle of Hpnotiq on the back bar is an immediate green flag. It tells me the bar is fun, has a sense of humor, and knows how to balance classic cocktail craft with a little playfulness. I love a serious cocktail program, but I love it even more when the people behind it know when to break the fourth wall and be a little less serious. A bottle of radioactive blue liqueur sitting next to your $90 amaro tells me you’re confident enough to be a little silly, which is exactly what I want in a bar. Not everything needs to be rare, bitter, or made by a monk. Sometimes it should just be blue.” —Andi Burrows, founder, Kayos Creative, Brooklyn

“I think that a bottle of Cascahuín tequila is a huge green flag. It means that the sourcing of spirits is intentional and that they aren’t also just going for what’s trending in terms of more traditionally made agave spirits. It’s also readily available for most of their SKUS and something any spirit loving bartender can get behind.” —Jonathan Adler, managing partner, Chiqui, NYC

“The bottle that almost always gives me that ‘green flag’ feeling is See The Elephant amaro. Produced in southern Italy, it uses arugula as its primary botanical, and all of the other herbs and botanicals are locally harvested. On its own, it smells like a freshly opened piece of Bazooka Joe bubble gum, which does not make any sense in the best way possible. The flavor notes are more akin to egg nog, which is both complex and polarizing. This is an obscure bottle for a lot of people, but any bar that carries it shows me it embraces unique things that most places may easily pass over.” —Max Schikora, bar manager, Echelon and Huna, Ann Arbor, Mich.

“Galliano is a fabulous and underutilized cocktail component. It’s also my go-to neat shooter, and it’s so much more than a vodka and orange juice accompaniment. To me, it signifies that the bar respects a retro classic, and it may even get adventurous with it. That, or it’s a relic that I’ll gladly chip away at when I visit. The bottle might not have been touched for the past decade, but it’s in the building, and therefore, it’s an option! I take comfort in that.” —Erica Luera, bartender, Strong Water, Anaheim, Calif.

“Rochelt Brandy is one of those bottles that if you know, you know. It’s ridiculously expensive, incredibly well-made, and so niche that most people don’t know what it is, including bartenders. So when I see it on a back bar, it’s a huge green flag. Chances are, whoever decided to carry it is a serious spirits geek who genuinely appreciates the craft. Rochelt isn’t something you just pick up on the job as a bartender. It’s something you discover because you’re genuinely a spirits geek who’s spent years seeking out and tasting things out of pure curiosity. It’s also not a bottle you stock to make money, it’s a bottle you stock because you know how special it is, and hope someone else walks in who does too.” —Vay Su, co-owner, Vandell, Los Angeles

“Chartreuse, green or yellow. I assume someone somewhere knows something if I see either of them. Bonus points if I spot them in a dive bar.” —Aaron Jones, beverage manager, Board & Batten, Mesa, Ariz.

“Tequila Tapatio 110. Overproof or still-proof tequila in general is a green flag because it means whoever is making choices for the program is paying attention to something other than price point or brand recognition. Tapatio 110 isn’t diluted, and it’s also delicious, and holds up in cocktails. The real bars know.” —Sid Lewis, bartender, Semiprecious, Denver

“Whenever I see shochu on the back bar or on the menu, I always get excited, because it’s a category that I really care about, and find so interesting and versatile. I love that it is being featured more and more on back bars. When I see Nikaido on a menu specifically, I’m more inclined to think that the bar team has experience working with shochu since it’s a more traditional brand with a low ABV. I also love the toastiness that Nikaido has as the result of being made with 100 percent barley. It tends to bring a beautiful, round flavor to a cocktail.” —A-K Hada, co-owner, dokidoki, Brooklyn

“I love tiki drinks, but I don’t necessarily love tiki bars. So any time I see Worthy Park 109 on the back bar, it’s a green flag that I’m in a bar that respects rum, and that I can trust them to make a decent Mai Tai or Jungle Bird. ‘Dark rum’ is such a vague category that’s been very limited for a long time, and Worthy Park really knocked it out of the, well, park, with this one.” —Tom Martinez, general manager, Bar Betsie, Washington, D.C.

“A bottle of Hypnotiq! Seeing it on the shelves tells me one of two things: The bar is either here for a good time or they’ve been here for a long time.” —Austin Harrington, bartender, Youngblood, San Diego

title: The Buildout Podcast: Rick Bayless
summary:
This episode of The Buildout is brought to you by Farmer’s Gin. As a bartender, I get to taste a lot of gin, so I can be picky about what I offer my guests. Farmer’s Gin is one of those bottles I keep coming back to, because it delivers exactly what I’m looking for behind the bar. It’s clean, balanced, and makes a fantastic Martini, but it also shines in classics like a Negroni, Gimlet, or even an Alaska. What I really appreciate is how many different drinkers it appeals to.

content:
This episode of The Buildout is brought to you by Farmer’s Gin. As a bartender, I get to taste a lot of gin, so I can be picky about what I offer my guests. Farmer’s Gin is one of those bottles I keep coming back to, because it delivers exactly what I’m looking for behind the bar. It’s clean, balanced, and makes a fantastic Martini, but it also shines in classics like a Negroni, Gimlet, or even an Alaska. What I really appreciate is how many different drinkers it appeals to. There’s enough juniper for London Dry fans, but also beautiful floral and citrus notes to win over those who prefer softer, more modern gins. It’s one of those bottles guests love because it just tastes great. If you care about quality and well-made cocktails, check out Farmer’s Gin. Follow them at @farmersgin or visit farmersgin.com.

Rick Bayless is one of America’s most celebrated chefs, known as much for championing local farmers and purveyors as he is for transforming the way Americans understand Mexican cuisine. Long before authentic Mexican cooking gained widespread recognition in the U.S., Bayless was determined to bring the flavors and traditions he fell in love with in Mexico to American diners. That passion led him to open Frontera Grill, a restaurant that would forever change the way Americans thought about Mexican food.

On this episode of “The Buildout,” Rick sits down with Adam to discuss his lifelong love affair with Mexico, the challenges of introducing authentic Mexican cuisine to American diners, and how he built one of the country’s most influential restaurant empires.

content:
Riesling is all but synonymous with German wine. It’s the most planted grape in Germany, accounting for almost a quarter of the country’s vineyard area. And while Riesling’s dominance is not about to change anytime soon, another white variety is becoming recognized for its quality and potential in Germany. The grape is none other than Chardonnay.

German Chardonnay is still a minor player, covering only about 3 percent of German vineyards. About 7,000 acres of it were under vine in 2023, but more of it is being planted every year. And with good reason. Many of the wines are spectacular and should gain traction as more people are exposed to them. And they satisfy the preferences of an increasing number of wine lovers.

For one thing, they have moderate levels of alcohol, with many in the 12 to 13 percent range. And most of the wines I tasted showed judicious use of oak, with the wood accenting rather than dominating. Because production is limited at this point, the wines are not inexpensive, with some in the $40 to $60 range. But the quality is instantly recognizable.

Chardonnay is grown primarily in the Rheinhessen, Pfalz, and Baden regions in the warmer southwest. And while Germany is still a cool-climate wine country, global warming has helped Chardonnay (and other varieties) achieve ripeness more easily.

“Germany put all their eggs in the Riesling basket, never thinking that Chardonnay could actually ripen,” says Collin Wagner, a sales manager with vom Boden, an importer of German wines. But now, in most years, Chardonnay does ripen. And the fruit in many of the wines is gorgeous, with ample acidity making them superbly refreshing and age-worthy.

Wagner says he believes Chardonnay is opening the door to Germany for more wine lovers because it’s simpler than Riesling to understand. Riesling, he says, “has this baggage of: ‘Is it dry? Is it off-dry? Is it shrill? I hate Riesling. I love Riesling. I don’t understand Riesling.’” Chardonnay, he maintains, “is more liked and lovable. And in a certain way it’s easier.”

While Chardonnay has a long history in Burgundy — the variety is thought to have originated there — it was only officially approved for planting in Germany in 1991. The wines have quickly become among the most exciting Chardonnays in the world. For some, the leanness of the wines calls to mind white Burgundies of the 1980s when that region had a cooler climate.

Here are seven of the best German Chardonnays:

Friedrich Becker Chardonnay 2025

This wine is slightly effervescent when first poured, but the spritz subsides with aeration and a complex Chardonnay emerges. There are lemon-lime, green apple, mint, and floral notes at first followed by touches of grapefruit, vanilla, and saline. The wine is aged in large oak casks so the wood influence is minimal. The fruit is both concentrated and refreshing. The vineyards are in Pfalz on the border with France’s Alsace.

Price: $27
Buy This Wine

Lukas Hammelmann ‘Aus den Dörfern Z’ Chardonnay 2025

Balanced and memorable with concentrated, ripe green and red apple notes, hints of Meyer lemon, mandarin, honeysuckle, minerals, and a wisp of cumin seed. Light, focused, and unencumbered by much oak. Aus den Dörfern means “from the villages” and Z refers to Zeiskam, Lukas Hammelmann’s hometown in the Pfalz. Hammelmann’s 2024 Chardonnay Roter Berg, a richer, somewhat deeper wine, is also worth seeking out.

Price: $48
Buy This Wine

Von Winning Chardonnay ‘Royale’ 2024

The fruit in this wine from Pfalz is concentrated but not cloying, with candied apple and pineapple aromas and flavors accented by herbs and baking spice notes. There’s a mineral hint and the oak is well integrated.

Price: $32
Buy This Wine

Knewitz Chardonnay 2023

A flinty nose introduces this Chardonnay from Rheinhessen along with a wisp of oak-driven butterscotch. But those initial notes settle down as the wine opens up, revealing green apple, stone fruit, and citrus flavors. The wine is light, precise, and delightful. Knewitz uses organic practices.

Price: $42
Buy This Wine

Jonas Dostert ‘Frost24’ Chardonnay 2024

This wine is from the Mosel region, where slate soils rule. But the grapes for this wine are grown in limestone. The wine is lean and nervy and aged in mostly used oak barrels, so the wood is there but subtle. It lands light-bodied on the palate, with green apple, tropical fruit, orange, and lemon notes.

Price: $44
Buy This Wine

Andreas Durst Chardonnay 2024

This lovely fruit-driven wine is marked by yellow and green apple and tangerine notes along with hints of mint and cream. Andreas Durst farms organically and by hand in Pfalz. He uses old barrels to age the wine, so the wood influence is muted. It’s an unusual, small-production wine.

Price: $60
Buy This Wine

Wasenhaus Chardonnay 2024

Subtle herb notes infuse this well-balanced Chardonnay from Baden with pear and apricot flavors and a subtle oak layer. A stony minerality punctuates the fruit, providing a texture that lasts through the long finish. It’s aged in both used oak barrels and stainless steel.

Price: $48
Buy This Wine

Next up: Red and white wines from France’s Bergerac

title: A Wine Cellar Was Left Untouched Since 1939. Here’s What Was Found
summary:

The article A Wine Cellar Was Left Untouched Since 1939. Here’s What Was Found appeared first on VinePair.
content:
John Smith had to actually buy the 10,600-square-foot stucco Tudor mansion before he would be able to open the wine cellar and find out what bottles had been left down there some 86 years earlier.

Hidden off the main road at the end of a circular driveway, The Sherman Estates was built on fifteen acres of land in northwest Dayton, Ohio in 1925. Its original owner was John Q. Sherman, the co-founder of the Standard Register Company as well as a prolific inventor who held over 190 patents.

Initially called The Highland, it was set on, yes, higher lands after the immense damage caused by the Great Dayton Flood of 1913. Its Zillow listing humbly mentioned six bedrooms, four full bathrooms, and two half baths, but that was a bit understated. In fact, the business magnate had filled his home with countless features he had enjoyed in the houses and castles he saw when traveling through Europe:

A butler’s pantry and breakfast nook, a grand staircase leading to the second floor, a solarium in the dead center of the home with a ceramic tile fountain, and French doors leading to an outdoor mirrored fountain and a grotto; a library, a billiards room, a three-car garage, and a then-state-of-the-art intra-room intercom system with handheld earphone and call pushbuttons.

The Great Room would offer a 30-foot high stucco cathedral ceiling with fleur-de-lis relief and king post beams, carved rosettes crown chandeliers dangling between them, and a fireplace ringed by a wrought-iron wrap with a leather seat. Sherman and his wife, Katherine, would fill the room with treasures befitting Charles Foster Kane — most notably, a Persian rug measuring 12 x 30 feet.

The Shermans had hosted a lot of fundraising parties in their heyday — Sherman was a big-time philanthropist who was a key founder of the University of Dayton as well as Good Samaritan Hospital — and there were 25 full settings of gold and silverware. At these parties, other bold faced Dayton names of the day like Orville Wright had tripped the light fantastic.

And, in an obscure corner of the house, at the bottom of a back staircase, underneath the stairs, was a wine cellar that had been sealed shut and never reopened since the year Sherman died — 1939.

Didn’t Even Know It Was There

If someone were to have bought this house and suddenly have access to the sealed cellar, you could do worse than Smith. He’s long had a fascination with alcohol in all categories, born to a father who made his own wine, he has brewed his own beer and mead. He drinks bourbon, Scotch, and rum. But he also loves home architecture from the days of the robber barons and captains of industry.

“Since I was a kid, I’ve always loved touring old houses and mansions,” says Smith. He recalls visiting Fallingwater in Pennsylvania and the Henry Clay Frick House in New York as a child. “So it’s kind of a lifelong dream for me to have a big mansion to restore.”

The opportunity would come after a recent retirement. Born near Pittsburgh, he attended the Air Force Academy and worked in the service his whole life. With his wife’s family located in Ohio, they decided to relocate there for their golden years. They had become aware of the Sherman Estate and its availability around 2023 when it was first put on the market by the Shermans’ remaining heirs. It had a great price then and even better one now, just around a half a million bucks.

Katherine had remained in the house until her death in 1965. Together the Shermans had eight children, the last of which would survive until 2020. But after 1965 no one exactly lived in the home except for a ground caretaker who never really touched the main house, so much so that Katherine still had jewelry and open letters on her nightstand decades after her death.

You might wonder why nothing was ever put up for an estate sale, but with eight kids and several dozen grandkids, there were just too many hands in the pie — a pie that would ultimately never get cut up. Eventually, however, the cost of holding onto this relic got to be too much and there was no choice but to sell. First to a holding company apparently owned by one of the Iams pet food heirs, in 2023. They never lived there either, however, and eventually offered it to the Smiths.

“So we went back out there to make an offer,” says Smith. “And the nice thing is all the big pieces of furniture and the key stuff that you would want in the house are still there. But they had never even opened the wine cellar door.

“I don’t even know if they knew it was there, man.”

Shock

Smith had caught a little glimpse of the cellar while first touring the house, but there was something wedged in the door so he was unable to fully check it out. The door itself really caught his attention — a cathedral door with a dozen or so square holes, inch by inch, in the top of it, surely for airflow.

Eventually, after closing on the home, Smith used his strength to get the door open. Inside the cellar it was total darkness. There was a musty, dank smell to it. Some surfaces were a bit damp.

“It was stuffed floor to ceiling with bottles. Bottles stacked on top of bottles on top of bottles,” he recalls. “I was just in shock.”

The bottles were extremely dusty with a sticky film over most of them. Some were stored on their sides, others were upright. It would take Smith nearly 48 hours to get all the bottles out and into better light, where he would discover all 400 or so were from the 1930s or earlier.

“Part of being well-heeled back then was being able to offer an impressive set of selections for people.”

There were 47 bottles of Niersteiner Rhine wine from 1895, 42 bottles of Chanson Père & Fils Sparkling Burgundy from 1934, 12 bottles of Tokaji Royal Blend wine produced in Austria-Hungary in 1895. There were 5 bottles of Barton & Guestier Haut Sauternes from the same era, 5 bottles of Old California Port from 1905, and 8 bottles of what appears to be “Fisson Frères Bordeaux Port,” though the exact name on the label is somewhat hard to decipher after so long.

There were bottles of Old Overholt rye from the 1910s, Prohibition-era Bourbon de Luxe from United Distillers, and three bottles of the legendary Golden Wedding Rye, an old Pennsylvania brand.

There was Prohibition-era non-alcoholic Old Town London Dry Gin, Ronrico Gold Label Puerto Rican Rum, and Hiram Walker’s Sloe Gin. There was Noilly Prat dry vermouth from 1934, grenadine, apricot syrup, blackberry cordial, and crème de cacao (with a “Great for Alexanders” motto on the neck label).

There were 100 Cuban cigars dating to the early 1900s as well, surprisingly not fully dried out.

There were Scotch flagons from 1896 and giant demijohns without labels that were presumably wine. Smith popped the cork on one and it didn’t smell like vinegar, a positive sign. He dipped his finger in and tasted it on his tongue — not bad.

Then Smith saw some strange wicker jugs he likewise thought might be wine. He spun the gallon size jugs around and there were cardboard tags around the necks:

CIA. “Ron Bacardi” S.A.
Sucesores de Bacardi y Comp.
Proveedores de la Real Casa de España
Santiago de Cuba

This was pre-Revolution, pre-Prohibition Cuban rum from around 1919 or so. And Smith had three bottles of it.

A Well-Heeled Collection

“It’s like Christmas here at Bacardi,” Rachel Dorion Guerin, a sixth-generation family member and the brand’s heritage curator, told Smith after she got her hands on one of his bottles. He had reached out to her on a whim, eventually selling the company one of the three bottles — one already opened and just half-full — for $1,000.

It’s hard to estimate what one of the full bottles might be worth on an open market as nothing of this type has ever exactly appeared for sale with auction houses or otherwise. A Bacardi Superior Carta de Oro from the era sold on the Rum Auctioneer website for £1,850.00 (around $2,500 USD) in 2023. However, that was a mere 24-ounce bottle lacking the wicker covering.

If Bacardi was founded in 1862, it initially didn’t sell rum in bottles at the outset, instead offering rum straight from the barrel into whatever containers customers brought with them. That said, founder Don Facundo Bacardí Massó was unusually early to branding his spirits; by 1873 he had a flagship expression, Ron Superior Extra Seco, and by 1909 a standardized bottle format. The oldest bottle currently at Bacardi headquarters dates to 1904, a small, unlabeled hip flask of Bacardi Carta Blanca.

The wicker covering is another story, initially used as an old shipping form to protect fragile, mouth-blown glass bottles on long transit. However, by the 1950s and on, the wicker had become more of an aesthetic choice, and countless, mostly empty examples of the “Palmas Extra” bottles distilled in Mexico and Puerto Rico are available on places like eBay and Etsy, selling cheaply for around $25 apiece.

The Bacardi company was pursuing the American market from the get-go, especially after the U.S. forced the Spanish out of Cuba in 1898. By the 1910s there was even an American bottling plant in New York. But with Smith’s bottle most likely being packaged right before or just at the start of Prohibition, Bacardi wouldn’t have been able to legally sell it in the country. So how did a rich man in Dayton, Ohio get several bottles of it?

“The wicker basket seems to have been a common thing for tourists buying somewhere in the Caribbean to take home,” says Matt Pietrek, a rum historian and most recently the author of “The Rum Never Sets.”

“It was stuffed floor to ceiling with bottles. Bottles stacked on top of bottles on top of bottles. I was just in shock.”

It’s most likely that the jet-setting Shermans had simply traveled to Cuba and brought the gorgeous bottles (and those 100 or so cigars) back as keepsakes. Like a lot of wealthy people of this era, having unique bottles to pour your guests would have been of great social value. I can’t help but recall what Joshua Feldman, a vintage spirits expert, had told me when I was writing “Dusty Booze: In Search of Vintage Spirits”:

“Part of being well-heeled back then was being able to offer an impressive set of selections for people.”

And, indeed, now that he himself is the ostensibly well-heeled owner of a mansion, Smith may use his remaining two demijohns to serve guests this more-than-100-year-old rum whenever he’s finally able to have them over to his new digs.

Maybe he’ll host a Roaring Twenties-themed party. Or perhaps he’ll open the Bacardi and other bottles at a charity dinner to help raise funds for the local schools, churches, hospitals, and universities the Shermans had once supported.

“Or, maybe once the house is finished,” he told me, “I’ll just find the biggest, oldest, comfiest chair in the house, pour myself a drink of one of the bottles, close my eyes, breathe deeply, and imagine the sights, sounds, and people of the early 1900s all around me — and enjoy making a dream come true.”

title: We Asked 8 Sommeliers: What’s the Most Overrated White Wine? (2026)
summary:
White wine is a reliable go-to for many drinkers. It can bring crisp, saline edges, juicy tropical fruit notes, or even rich, nutty flavors. For its diversity, palatability, and low-ABV nature, the genre has recently seen a boost in appeal. But along with that growing popularity, some grapes, regions, or bottles tend to take more than their fair share of the spotlight. And the bottles that drum up the most excitement might not always be all they are hyped up to be.

The article We Asked 8 Sommeliers: What’s the Most Overrated White Wine? (2026) appeared first on VinePair.
content:
White wine is a reliable go-to for many drinkers. It can bring crisp, saline edges, juicy tropical fruit notes, or even rich, nutty flavors. For its diversity, palatability, and low-ABV nature, the genre has recently seen a boost in appeal.

But along with that growing popularity, some grapes, regions, or bottles tend to take more than their fair share of the spotlight. And the bottles that drum up the most excitement might not always be all they are hyped up to be. Consumers each have their own preferences, but sometimes it’s worth looking past the wines receiving major recognition to discover a new hidden gem.

That’s why we tapped eight sommeliers from around the country to name the white wines they think are the most overrated. From a certain Loire Valley region that many consider overpriced to butter-bomb Chardonnays, here’s what they had to say.

The most overrated white wines, according to sommeliers:

  • Sancerre
  • Go-to white wines
  • Pinot Grigio
  • Buttery California Chardonnay
  • Muscat
  • Yellow Tail Chardonnay
  • Pinot Gris

“The most overrated white wine has to be Sancerre — not because it is not one of the most famously delicious expressions of Sauvignon Blanc known to the world for centuries, but because there are so many other wonderful things coming from the Loire Valley. Menatou Salon often offers Sauvignon Blancs that, in my opinion, drink closer to Sancerre these days than one may want to believe (Domaine Pellé’s Morogues Blanc, for example). Sancerre sets the stage and creates a wonderful point of departure for a world of crisp citrus and mineral-driven white wines that can also be found in Austria, Italy, and many other white wine growing regions of France. We are always happy to help Sancerre drinkers find an alternative they never knew they loved.” —Sam Stresing, wine director, Lowland, Charleston, S.C.

“The most overrated white wine isn’t a particular grape or region, but the one you choose on autopilot. I’m a big believer in drinking whatever you love, but we give the same handful of whites far too much attention when there’s an entire world of incredible wines out there. I love Chardonnay as much as the next girl, but give Godello a chance!” —Emily Nevin-Giannini, senior beverage director, Barcelona Wine Bar, Norwalk, Conn.

“Pinot Grigio is the most overrated white wine. There are some not-so-great representations out there that get outsized attention. But fear not! There are some awesome wines made from Pinot Grigio from all over the world, including Italy, the U.S., Australia, New Zealand, and France!” —Barb Werley, master sommelier, Nuri Steakhouse, Dallas

“I’m more drawn to crisp, refreshing flavors like green apple and citrus, with stainless steel or neutral oak aging that keeps the wine balanced and easy to drink. I’m happy to see the trend moving away from the heavy, buttery California Chardonnays that were so popular for years. Sometimes all that oak can overpower the fruit, so it’s nice to see more wineries letting the wine speak for itself and keeping things fresh.” —Austin Krudys, beverage manager, The Chloe, Nashville

“Muscat and its related varieties (Moscatel, Moscato, etc.) have a long history of producing beautiful wines across a range of styles, from the Mediterranean to Japan. Personally, though, I often find the pronounced white floral aromas overpowering, making this a grape family I tend not to gravitate toward. That’s a matter of personal taste rather than a reflection of the quality or diversity of these wines.” —Sarah MacIsaac, wine director, Nautilus Pier 4, Boston

“As of October 2026, the world’s most overrated white wine has to be Sancerre. Production has been pushed to the max in order to meet demand, significantly diluting quality while prices have continued to increase. (But I can’t exactly blame producers for trying to capitalize on the Sancerre craze). Outside of a few key producers like Vatan, the wine is decidedly mediocre, especially when you consider the universe of other great white wines available: Vinho Verde, Albariño, Aussie Riesling, Willamette Valley Chardonnay, South African Chenin. I could go on forever.” —Evan White, wine director, Bludorn Hospitality, Houston

“Yellow Tail Chardonnay is a classic example of brand recognition doing more work than the wine itself. It’s familiar, inexpensive, and easy to find, but ‘familiar’ isn’t the same as ‘good.’ Spend a couple of dollars more, and you can usually find a Chardonnay with brighter acidity, cleaner fruit, better balance, and less heavy oak or residual sweetness … something more refreshing, distinctive, and food-friendly than this soft crowd-pleaser.” —Emelio Sansone, executive chef, Tin Lizzie Lounge, Seattle

“At the moment, the most overrated white wine is Pinot Gris. I would much rather guide a guest to a variety of other aromatic whites ranging from Riesling to Zibibbo depending on their stylistic preferences. There’s just so much more interesting wine available to try.” —William Jones, chief operating officer and wine director, Deep Roots Restaurant Group, Fairhope, Ala.
